title: Lesson 2 Quiz: Analyze Evidence and Compare Policy Options
description: A short quiz to check what you learned in this lesson. Submitting it completes the lesson's quiz requirement, and your score is recorded separately.

history.note: AI-written question draft. Not reviewed or approved by a human (admin); do not give to students.

Comprehensive audit: q2 replaced by a numeric difference-in-differences item (same id) so the quiz covers the lesson's research-method objective; q4 difficulty set to intermediate. Not reviewed or approved by a human.

questions.prompt: A student finds the claim "Our filters cut school absences by half" on a filter company's website, with no study cited. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Use the claim as it is, because a company knows more about its own products than anyone else does.
Look for an independent study or official data, because the company gains if readers believe the claim.
Reject the claim and the product, because information from companies is usually false or misleading.
Use the claim but round the number down a little, so that the project does not overstate the effect.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Schools that joined a tutoring program raised the share of students passing a reading test from 52% to 70% over two years. Similar schools that did not join went from 50% to 61% over the same two years. Assuming both groups would have followed parallel paths without the program, what is the difference-in-differences estimate of the program's effect, in percentage points? (Enter a number only; for example, enter 5 for 5 percentage points.)

Hypothetical example: A literacy program costs $36,000. An evaluation with a comparison group estimates that it raises the number of students who reach a minimum reading level by 450. What is the program's cost per additional student reaching that level, in dollars? (Enter a number only.)

Hypothetical example: Two options cost the same and improve school water supply equally. Option P is paid for by a flat fee of the same amount per household; Option Q is paid for by a progressive income tax. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Option P places a larger burden, relative to income, on low-income households than Option Q does.
Option P is fairer, because each household pays the same dollar amount.
The two options have the same effects on each income group, because their average costs are equal.
Option Q is regressive, because higher-income households pay more dollars in total under it.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: Option A costs $40 per extra student-day if take-up is 80%, but $70 if take-up is 40%. Option B costs $55 per extra student-day whatever the take-up. Local take-up is unknown. What is the best way to present the recommendation?

choices.text: Recommend Option A, because its best-case figure is the lowest number in the whole comparison.
Recommend Option B, because its cost per day does not depend on how many students take part.
Say that A is better only if take-up is high enough, and name the evidence that would settle it.
Average A's two figures and compare the result, $55, with B's $55 to show that they are equal.
